greeting: Good morning, Yamuna. This week the Van Eyck portraits and a Renoir video from the National Gallery look made for a slow weekend, with Alan Garner's Red Shift waiting for your drive.

literature.why: A conversation about a novel's layered, history-haunted storytelling and the force of its narrative voice, which is just your territory, and the hour suits a drive.
A first-person narrator and a piece of history that no essay could convey so directly: Melvyn Bragg and guests on a voice worth hearing.
A biography whose very title pairs art with life, a lovely fit for your interest in how painting and fiction speak to each other.
A short, appreciative essay on lyrical, musical prose, for a quiet moment when you want language that is simply beautiful.

art.why: An hour with a co-curator walking you through the Van Eyck show is ideal for the car, and the auction-week chatter is a pleasant bonus.
A change of painter and mood: Renoir's love-themed paintings, guided by the curators who know them best, and easy to enjoy by ear.
Since you will already have heard about Van Eyck, this review adds the pleasure of vivid, carefully made prose about the paintings themselves.
A sixteenth-century book of apocalyptic omens, with a wonderfully modern 'doomscrolling' comparison: strange, visual and made for storytelling.

watch.why: A painting, a missing woman and a story waiting to be told: Tissot's canvas read almost like a novel's opening, and it is on Arte.
As a literature teacher you may enjoy hearing contemporary French writers talk about Woolf's essay, in conversation rather than on the page.
History told through women's own voices, much as a good novel would tell it, and the full film is free on Arte.
A gentler cultural detour on Disney+, and a pleasing companion to this week's doll-themed Arte film.

world.why: A novel about Ravel and Vaughan Williams, discussed on Start the Week: fiction, music and friendship across borders, ideal for a drive.
A single place and its buried history, told as a documentary: the kind of story that teaches more than an essay.
Selkies, family memory and Irish folklore in one essay: a story you can step into without needing the background first.
A physicist, lost birdsong and music: a short, gentle piece for someone who loves beautiful sound.
